analogy.p: Imagine a jigsaw puzzle where several pieces have gone missing. Because the pattern around each hole is clear, you can work out what the missing piece must look like (its colours and shape) before you ever find it. Mendeleev’s gaps worked in just the same way: the elements above, below and beside each gap told him what the missing element should be like, and when gallium and germanium turned up they matched. The analogy breaks down because jigsaw pieces have one fixed shape, whereas Mendeleev’s predictions were only **approximate**, and he also had to **swap a few ‘pieces’ around** because atomic weight, his main ordering rule, turned out to be the wrong property.

bullets: The two ways early chemists tried to sort elements were by their **properties** (metal or non-metal, how they react, what compounds they form) and by their **atomic weight** (now called **relative atomic mass, Ar**).
A good classification does three jobs: it **organises** known facts, it reveals **patterns**, and it lets you make **predictions** that can be tested.

In this specification you need to know: early attempts to classify elements, why early tables were problematic, how **Mendeleev** improved on them, how his predictions were confirmed, and how knowledge of **isotopes** and **atomic number** explained the remaining problems.
The modern table is arranged in order of **atomic (proton) number**, in **groups** (columns) and **periods** (rows).

Keep the story as a chain of cause and effect: early tables had problems, so Mendeleev changed the method, so predictions were possible, so the table was accepted, so later knowledge (isotopes) explained the leftover oddities.
core.h: 1. What the periodic table is and why scientists needed one
core.p: By the early 1800s chemists had discovered dozens of elements and noticed that some behaved very similarly (for example lithium, sodium and potassium all react vigorously with water). A **classification** was needed so that the properties of known elements could be organised, patterns spotted, and the behaviour of new elements predicted. The **periodic table** is that classification: the elements are arranged so that elements with **similar properties** end up in the same **column**. The development of the table is also a classic example of how **scientific ideas change** as new evidence arrives.

bullets: **Atomic weight** is the old name for **relative atomic mass (Ar)**. The two terms are used for the same idea, and exam questions may use either.
Early scientists did **not** know about the structure of the atom, so they could not use **atomic number** (number of protons). That is the root of most early problems.

Döbereiner (early 1800s) noticed ‘triads’: groups of three similar elements where the middle element’s atomic weight was roughly the average of the other two (for example lithium, sodium, potassium or chlorine, bromine, iodine). This showed that atomic weight and properties are linked, but it only covered a few elements.
Many early tables were **incomplete** because many elements had not been discovered yet, and some atomic weights were measured **inaccurately**.

Early tables also tended to be drawn as simple lists with no way of showing that a pattern repeated, which is why the idea of **periodicity** (a pattern repeating at regular intervals) was so important.
core.h: 2. Early attempts: classifying by properties and by atomic weight
core.p: The earliest classifications simply split elements into **metals** and **non-metals**. Once chemists could measure **atomic weights** (the mass of an atom compared with a standard), the obvious next step was to list elements in **order of atomic weight** and look for repeating patterns. Atomic weight was the only measurable ‘size’ of an atom at the time, because nobody yet knew about protons, neutrons or electrons.

bullets: Example: counting lithium as 1, sodium is the **8th** element and potassium the **15th**, and all three are soft, reactive metals. Fluorine and chlorine also line up and are both reactive non-metals.
The pattern **worked for the lighter elements** only, up to about calcium. After that it broke down.

Newlands **did not leave gaps** for undiscovered elements, so he forced known elements into places where they did not belong, putting elements with **different properties** in the same column (a famous example is iron placed with oxygen and sulfur).
The **noble gases had not been discovered**, so there was no place for them in his scheme.
His ideas were **not widely accepted** at the time, partly because they could not explain the problems above and partly because there was no theory about why elements might behave periodically.
Exam point: Newlands’ table was **incomplete** and kept strictly to atomic-weight order even where properties clearly did not match.
core.p: John Newlands arranged the known elements in **order of atomic weight** and noticed that **every eighth element** had similar properties to the first, like the eighth note in a musical octave. He called this the **law of octaves**. It was a genuine step forward because it was the first clear statement that properties **repeat periodically** when elements are listed by atomic weight.

bullets: **Incomplete**: many elements (such as gallium, germanium and the noble gases) were still undiscovered, so the pattern looked broken.
**Strict atomic-weight order** placed some elements with others they did not resemble, because atomic weight does not always increase in step with the chemical behaviour of an element.
Some **atomic weights were inaccurate**, so elements could be in the wrong order.
There was **no explanation** for periodicity: nobody knew that it comes from the **arrangement of electrons** in atoms.
Because of these problems, scientists were not convinced the pattern was real; a table is only useful if it can **explain** and **predict**.
core.p: The specification states that **early periodic tables were incomplete** and that, if **strict atomic-weight order** was followed, **some elements were placed in inappropriate groups**. These two ideas are the key to explaining why a better table was needed and what Mendeleev did differently.

bullets: He arranged elements in **rows and columns** (the forerunner of periods and groups) so that **elements with similar properties** shared a column.
He **left gaps** in the table for elements that he believed had **not yet been discovered**.
In a few places he **swapped the order** of elements so they fitted the pattern of their properties, rather than strictly following atomic weight (see section 7).
He **predicted the properties** of the missing elements from the elements above and below the gap.
He believed the **properties** of elements were more reliable than the measured atomic weights, and he suggested some atomic weights had been measured wrongly.
Result: his table had **no forced misplacements** and could be **tested**, which made it far more convincing than earlier versions.
core.p: Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist, also arranged the elements mainly in **order of atomic weight**, but he put **chemical properties first**. He placed elements with similar properties (and similar compounds) into the same **column**, and he was willing to break the strict order whenever properties demanded it. This flexibility was his key advantage over earlier attempts.

bullets: He called the missing element below aluminium ‘**eka-aluminium**’, predicting a relative atomic mass of about **68**. The element **gallium** was discovered in **1875** and fitted the prediction very closely (Ar about 69.7).

He called the missing element below silicon ‘**eka-silicon**’, predicting Ar about **72**, a density of about **5.5 g/cm³**, an oxide of formula XO2 and a chloride XCl4 that would be a liquid with a low boiling point. **Germanium**, discovered in **1886**, has Ar about 72.6, density about 5.3 g/cm³, an oxide GeO2 and a liquid chloride GeCl4.
A third gap, below boron (‘eka-boron’), was filled by **scandium** (1879).
Each successful prediction was **independent evidence**: the table was not just a tidy way of arranging known facts, it **predicted new facts**.
Scientific reasoning: a theory that makes **testable predictions that come true** is much more likely to be accepted than one that only describes existing data.
**Link to evaluation**: predictions were not perfect (the numbers were close, not identical), but being close is enough to show the pattern is genuine.
core.h: 6. Gaps and predictions: why they mattered
core.p: The brilliance of Mendeleev’s approach was that the **gaps made predictions**. Because the missing elements sat below known elements, he could estimate their atomic weight, their density, the formula of their oxide and chloride, and so on. When elements with **matching properties** were later discovered, scientists realised the table reflected a real pattern in nature. This is the evidence that convinced the scientific community.

bullets: **Tellurium and iodine**: Ar of Te is about **127.6** and Ar of I is about **126.9**. By weight alone iodine would come first, putting it in the oxygen/sulfur family and tellurium among the halogens. Mendeleev swapped them so each sat in the correct group.

**Argon and potassium** (a pair that became clear once argon was discovered in the 1890s): Ar of argon is about **39.9** and Ar of potassium about **39.1**. By weight potassium would come first, but argon is an unreactive noble gas and potassium is a reactive alkali metal, so argon must come **before** potassium.
**Cobalt and nickel** are another pair where the order by weight (about 58.9 and 58.7) does not match the order that fits their properties.
Mendeleev trusted **properties** over atomic weight; later work showed he was right to do so (section 8).
In exams the model idea is: ‘he **changed the order** of some elements so they fitted the pattern of their **properties** rather than their atomic weight’.
This is not cheating: it is a scientist recognising that **atomic weight is not the true ordering property**.
core.h: 7. Changing the order: the swapped pairs
core.p: Where strict atomic-weight order put an element in a group of the wrong chemical family, Mendeleev **reversed** the two elements. The best known example is **tellurium (Te)** and **iodine (I)**: tellurium has the slightly higher Ar (127.6) than iodine (126.9), but iodine clearly behaves like chlorine and bromine (Group 7), so it must come **after** tellurium in the table.

bullets: **Isotopes** are atoms of the same element with the **same number of protons** but a **different number of neutrons**.

Ar is an **average** and is affected by how many neutrons each isotope has and how common each isotope is. An element with fewer protons can end up with a **higher average mass** if its common isotopes contain many neutrons.

Example: argon is mostly argon-40 (18 protons, 22 neutrons) while potassium is mostly potassium-39 (19 protons, 20 neutrons). Potassium has **more protons** but a **lower average mass** because its common isotope has fewer neutrons.
Chemical properties depend on the **number and arrangement of electrons**, which equals the number of **protons** in a neutral atom; neutron number barely affects chemistry.

The key idea is that **atomic number** (the number of protons) is the correct ordering property. Ordering by atomic number **removes all the swapped pairs**: argon (18) comes before potassium (19), tellurium (52) comes before iodine (53).

Atomic number was established early in the 1900s (Moseley’s X-ray work around 1913 showed the elements really do fall in a sequence of whole numbers), which confirmed Mendeleev’s decisions to swap pairs.
So: Mendeleev **ordered by atomic weight but corrected using properties**; the modern table **orders by atomic number**, which explains why his corrections were needed.
core.h: 8. Isotopes and atomic number explain the anomalies
core.p: The specification says that **knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct**. Atomic weight (relative atomic mass) is a **weighted mean** of the masses of all the naturally occurring **isotopes** of an element. It therefore depends on the **neutron** content and the **abundance** of each isotope, not on the **number of protons**, which is what really determines the element and its chemistry.

bullets: **Atomic number** = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom, and it increases by one each step along a period.
**Group number** = **number of electrons in the outer shell** (Groups 1 to 7). Group 0 (noble gases) have a **full outer shell** (2 for helium, 8 for the rest).
**Period number** = **number of occupied electron shells**. Example: sodium (2,8,1) has three shells so it is in **Period 3**, and one outer electron so it is in **Group 1**.
Between Group 2 and Group 3 sits the block of **transition metals**.

Elements **change from metals to non-metals** across a period, and the metals are on the left and towards the bottom, non-metals on the right and towards the top (see the note on metals and non-metals).
Reading position from an electronic structure: **2,8,5** has three shells and five outer electrons, so it is in **Period 3, Group 5** (phosphorus, atomic number 15).
Elements in the same group show a **trend** down the group because the outer electrons are further from the nucleus as shells are added.
core.h: 9. The modern periodic table: how it is organised
core.p: In the modern periodic table the elements are arranged in **order of atomic (proton) number**. **Rows** are called **periods** and **columns** are called **groups**. Elements in the same group have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**, which is why they have **similar chemical properties**. The group number (for Groups 1 to 7 and 0) tells you the number of outer-shell electrons, and the period number tells you how many electron shells are occupied.

bullets: Noble gases are **chemically inert** because they already have a **full outer shell** of electrons.
They fit between the **Group 7 halogen** at the end of one period and the **Group 1 alkali metal** at the start of the next, e.g. chlorine, argon, potassium.
This is why **argon sits before potassium** even though its Ar is slightly higher (section 7).
Adding Group 0 is another example of the table being **flexible and predictive**.
Link: the unreactivity of noble gases is explained by their electronic structure, a theme that connects this topic to bonding and ionic compounds.
core.h: 10. Noble gases: a new group fitted in
core.p: Mendeleev’s original table had **no group for the noble gases** because they had not been discovered. They are very unreactive and make up only a tiny fraction of air, so they were found late, in the **1890s**. When they were discovered they could be added as a **new column (Group 0)** on the end of the table **without disturbing the existing arrangement**. That the table could take in a whole new family without being rearranged was strong extra support for the underlying pattern.

bullets: **Gaps**: Newlands left none; Mendeleev **left gaps and predicted properties**; the modern table has no unexplained gaps in the main body.
**Noble gases**: not in Newlands’ or Mendeleev’s original tables; **added as Group 0** later and present in the modern table.
**Explanation**: neither Newlands nor Mendeleev could explain why properties repeat; the modern table is explained by **electron arrangement** (outer-shell electrons).
**Range**: Newlands’ pattern worked only for the lighter elements; Mendeleev’s worked for the known elements and predicted new ones.
**Acceptance**: Newlands was largely ignored; Mendeleev’s table was accepted once predictions were confirmed.
core.h: 11. Comparing Newlands, Mendeleev and the modern table
core.p: A comparison question may ask you to say what Mendeleev did better than earlier scientists or how the modern table differs. The points below help you organise the comparison. **Ordering**: Newlands strictly used atomic weight; Mendeleev mainly atomic weight but **adjusted using properties**; the modern table uses **atomic number**.

bullets: Mendeleev’s table **explained** known patterns in properties.
It made **testable predictions** (gallium, germanium, scandium) that later experiments **confirmed**.
The results were **repeatable**: other scientists could measure the properties of the new elements and check them against his predictions.
The table was **improved** when new evidence (noble gases, atomic number, isotopes) arrived, rather than being thrown away.
Scientists did not accept the idea on authority: acceptance followed the **evidence**, which is the key phrase mark schemes reward.
Another good phrase: it was ‘**peer reviewed and independently verified** by other scientists’.
Newlands’ ideas lacked this: they gave **no predictions** and had obvious flaws, so they were **not accepted**.
core.h: 12. How scientific ideas are accepted (evaluation skills)
core.p: Exam questions often ask **why Mendeleev’s table was accepted** even though it was not perfect. This is really a question about the scientific method. A scientific model is judged by whether it **explains existing observations** and **makes predictions that are later confirmed by experiment**.

bullets: To estimate a missing value in a group, you can take the **average of the elements above and below** (as Mendeleev effectively did) or read the **trend** down the group and extrapolate.
From an **electronic structure** you can deduce period and group (see section 9).

From **properties** you can deduce group: a reactive soft metal that floats on water and forms a +1 ion is **Group 1**; a coloured diatomic non-metal that forms a –1 ion is **Group 7**; a colourless, unreactive gas is **Group 0**.
Use **ranges and trends** in your answer (for example, ‘density increases down the group’) and always say **why** where you can.
When a graph of Ar against atomic number is plotted, the points rise almost steadily but with a **few dips** (Te and I, Ar and K, Co and Ni) which show why Ar is **not** a reliable ordering property.
Check units: density in g/cm³ and Ar has **no units**.
core.h: 13. Using the periodic table to predict and to interpret data
core.p: A top-grade answer shows you can **use** the table, not just recall its history. You may be given a set of data for elements in a group or a gap and asked to predict a missing value, or to say which group an element belongs to from its properties or electronic structure.

bullets: **Electronic structure**: the shell filling that explains groups and periods.
**Groups 1, 7 and 0**: the family trends that are the main payoff of arranging elements in columns.
**Metals and non-metals**: their position, how they form ions and how they differ in properties.
**Bonding**: ionic compounds form between metals (left) and non-metals (right); the group number predicts the **charge on the ion**.
**Working scientifically**: models change when new evidence is found, and predictions are used to test ideas.
core.p: This topic connects to many other parts of the specification, so examiners can mix it into longer questions about bonding, structure and reactivity. **Atomic structure**: protons, neutrons and electrons, isotopes, and relative atomic mass (Ar) calculations.

exam: **Command words**: ‘Describe’ = say what happened (facts); ‘Explain’ = give reasons using ‘because’; ‘Suggest’ = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation; ‘Evaluate’ = weigh up evidence for and against.
**1-mark questions** often ask for a single fact: ‘Why did Mendeleev leave gaps?’ Answer: ‘for undiscovered elements’. ‘What order are elements in the modern table?’ Answer: ‘atomic (proton) number’.
**2-mark questions**: one point plus a reason. Model: ‘Mendeleev **left gaps** (1) because he predicted **undiscovered elements** that would fit there (1).’
**3-4 mark ‘explain why Mendeleev’s table was accepted’**: gaps left, properties predicted, elements later discovered matched the predictions, so the table was supported by evidence.
**‘Why were early tables not accepted?’** Give two reasons: they were **incomplete**, and strict **atomic-weight order** put **elements with different properties** in the same group.
**‘Why is atomic-weight order not always correct?’** Answer with isotopes: Ar is an average mass that depends on **neutrons and isotope abundance**, not **protons**.
**Data question**: if you are given properties of elements either side of a gap, **find the pattern (trend or average)** and quote numbers from the data in your answer.
**Use the right terms**: group, period, atomic number, relative atomic mass, outer-shell electrons, isotopes. Do not write ‘atomic mass number’ for atomic number.

**6-mark extended answer**: plan a short structure: (1) problems with early tables, (2) what Mendeleev did (order, gaps, swaps), (3) predictions confirmed, (4) isotopes and atomic number explain the swaps. Link each step with ‘so’ or ‘because’.
Always give an **example** (gallium / germanium, tellurium / iodine, argon / potassium) when the question says ‘give an example’; one worked example earns a mark that a general statement does not.

mistakes.r: He arranged them mainly in order of **atomic weight** and adjusted using **chemical properties**; atomic number (protons) was not known until later and is used in the **modern** table.
mistakes.w: Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of atomic number.

mistakes.r: He left gaps **on purpose** for elements he **predicted had not yet been discovered**, and he **predicted their properties**.
mistakes.w: Mendeleev left gaps because he could not find the elements.

mistakes.r: It was accepted because the **predicted properties matched** the elements later discovered (e.g. gallium, germanium), which is **evidence**.
mistakes.w: His table was accepted just because it was neat.

mistakes.r: They worked only for the **lighter elements** (up to about calcium); **different elements were placed in the same group** and **no gaps** were left.
mistakes.w: Newlands’ octaves worked for all the elements.

mistakes.r: **Group** number = outer-shell electrons; **period** number = number of occupied **shells**.
mistakes.w: Period number equals the number of outer electrons.

mistakes.r: They were **not yet discovered**; once found they were added as a **new group (Group 0)** without upsetting the rest of the table.
mistakes.w: Noble gases were in Mendeleev’s original table.

mistakes.r: Knowledge of **isotopes** explains why **atomic-weight order was not always correct** (Ar is an average that depends on neutrons).
mistakes.w: Isotopes are why Mendeleev left gaps.

mistakes.r: He swapped (e.g. **tellurium and iodine**) so each element sat in the group matching its **chemical properties**.
Atomic number is the number of **protons** in the nucleus.
mistakes.w: Atomic number is the number of neutrons or the mass number.

summary: The specification asks you to describe how early chemists classified elements by atomic weight and properties, why early tables were incomplete and sometimes misplaced elements, how Mendeleev left gaps, predicted properties and reversed some orders, and how knowledge of isotopes and atomic number explains the anomalies. It matters because it shows how scientific models are tested and improved with evidence, and it underpins every later use of the periodic table.

terms.d: A table of elements arranged in order of atomic number, in groups (columns) and periods (rows), so that elements with similar properties are in the same column.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in a group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell and so similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. The period number is the number of occupied electron shells.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; the modern table is arranged in order of this number.
The old name for relative atomic mass; the weighted mean mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The average mass of the atoms of an element, taking into account the abundance of its isotopes, compared with carbon-12. It has no units.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
The 1864 idea that when elements are listed in order of atomic weight, every eighth element has similar properties.
The 1869 table that arranged elements mainly by atomic weight but according to properties, left gaps for undiscovered elements and sometimes reversed the order.
A space left in Mendeleev’s table for an element not yet found, whose properties he predicted from neighbouring elements.
The repeating pattern of properties of elements at regular intervals when the elements are placed in order.
Very unreactive gases with a full outer shell of electrons, discovered after Mendeleev’s first table and added as a new group.
Electrons in the highest occupied energy level of an atom; their number equals the group number for Groups 1 to 7 and decides chemical properties.
The block of metals between Group 2 and Group 3 of the periodic table.
A statement of what will happen or be found, based on a model, which can be tested by experiment.
Mendeleev’s name for the then-undiscovered element below silicon; it was later found and named germanium.

worked.ans: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties. When gallium and germanium were discovered, their properties matched his predictions, so the table was supported by evidence. He also swapped the order of some elements so that each was in the group matching its chemical properties, which earlier tables had not done.
worked.q: Explain why scientists accepted Mendeleev’s periodic table when earlier tables had not been accepted. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: Mendeleev **left gaps** for elements not yet discovered.
Mark 2: He **predicted the properties** of the missing elements from the elements around the gaps.
Mark 3: When new elements (such as **gallium and germanium**) were discovered, their properties **matched** his predictions.
Mark 4: He **reversed the order** of some elements so they fitted the pattern of their properties, so there were **fewer misplaced elements** than in earlier tables.

worked.ans: Estimated Ar of germanium = 73.4. This is within about 1 % of the real value of 72.6, so averaging the neighbours gives a good prediction (the pattern in the table is reliable). Ar has no units.
worked.q: Mendeleev predicted the relative atomic mass of the element below silicon (germanium) by using its neighbours. Silicon has Ar = 28.1 and tin has Ar = 118.7. Estimate the Ar of germanium by averaging, and compare it with the real value of 72.6. (3 marks)
steps: Divide by 2 to find the mean: 146.8 ÷ 2 = 73.4.

worked.ans: The table is ordered by atomic number. Argon (18 protons) comes before potassium (19 protons). Relative atomic mass is an average depending on the isotopes and their neutrons, so it is not a reliable way of ordering the elements.
worked.q: Argon (Ar = 39.9) comes before potassium (Ar = 39.1) in the modern periodic table, even though argon has the higher relative atomic mass. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: Mark 1: The modern table is in order of **atomic number (number of protons)**, not relative atomic mass.
Mark 2: Argon has 18 protons and potassium has 19, so argon comes first.
Mark 3: Ar is an **average** that depends on the **isotopes** present: argon’s common isotope has more neutrons, so its average mass is higher even though it has fewer protons.
